A1.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, but some data could be helpful if it genuinely improves outreach. Sensitive attributes are a risk unless fairness can demonstrably improve.
A1.notes.Q4: Explainability builds trust with students and allows for better targeted advice. A black box model isn't helpful for proactive support.
A1.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial. Prioritizing equal recall ensures we don’t widen achievement gaps, even if it means slightly fewer total identifications.
A1.notes.Q6: Personalized contact & invites are more effective, but respectful of student time. Twice a year feels like a reasonable frequency for proactive check-ins.
A1.notes.Q7: More personalized interventions justify broader reach; fewer false positives are key when offering individual support.
A1.Q8.1: The model’s impact on student agency is a concern - ensuring outreach doesn't feel intrusive or stigmatizing is critical.

A2.notes.Q3: Balancing privacy is key, but some data helps identify students at risk. Sensitive data needs a stronger justification and focus on fairness.
A2.notes.Q4: Explainability is critical for building trust with students and advisors. Less explainable models are hard to justify in intervention.
A2.notes.Q5: Fairness matters hugely. We can't perpetuate inequalities, even if it slightly impacts overall identification rates. Recall is key – don’t miss students.
A2.notes.Q6: Personalized support is best, but needs advisor time. Voluntary meetings are good; avoid overwhelming students with constant contact.
A2.notes.Q7: More selective for personalized intervention. A generic email is okay to cast a wider net, but we want targeted support, not just noise.
A2.Q8.1: The survey doesn’t really touch on the workload implications of implementing such a system. We need resources to handle increased outreach effectively.

A3.notes.Q3: Data privacy is paramount, but some additions clearly benefit students. Sensitive data requires strong justification and fairness focus.
A3.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for building trust with students & advisors. A black box model isn’t helpful, even if accurate. Some loss of accuracy for clarity is acceptable.
A3.notes.Q5: Fairness must be prioritized; reinforcing existing inequalities isn't acceptable. A slight decrease in overall identification for equitable outcomes is worthwhile.
A3.notes.Q6: Personalized contact and advisor meetings are best, but manageable frequency is important to avoid overwhelming students.
A3.notes.Q7: A tailored approach with more detailed intervention warrants a slightly broader net. Basic info outreach can be more targeted.
A3.Q8.1: It would be useful to know *how* the model will handle edge cases and unusual student profiles. Also, long-term monitoring of fairness is crucial.

S1.notes.Q3: Privacy is important, but knowing my own history, a little help earlier on could have saved me time and money. First-gen status and financial aid *might* be relevant for support needs.
S1.notes.Q4: Explainability is key, especially after dropping out once before. Knowing *why* I'm flagged helps me understand if the support is relevant. Less accuracy for more transparency feels right.
S1.notes.Q5: Fairness matters a lot to me, and I don't want this system reinforcing existing inequalities. A small loss in overall identification is worth it if it means equal opportunities.
S1.notes.Q6: A generic email feels impersonal; a personalized message shows they've actually looked at my situation. An invitation to meet is good too, but not overwhelming.
S1.notes.Q7: With a simple email outreach it’s okay to be broad. But personalized contact shouldn't waste anyone's time – fewer, targeted contacts are better.
S1.Q8.1: It would be good to know how this model interacts with existing support systems and whether students can opt-out entirely, not just ignore the messages.

S2.notes.Q3: Adding data can be helpful, but the risk of privacy violations feels high. As an international student who works, my financial status and nationality are particularly sensitive.
S2.notes.Q4: Explainability is important to build trust. I'd want an advisor understanding *why* the model flagged me, not just that it did. But a small loss of accuracy for more explainability is okay.
S2.notes.Q5: Fairness across groups should be a priority. I wouldn't want the system to disadvantage students from certain backgrounds, even if it means fewer total identifications.
S2.notes.Q6: Proactive support is good, but not overwhelming. Too much contact could be intrusive. A personalized email seems best – more effective than a generic one.
S2.notes.Q7: With general information, contacting more students is acceptable. But for personalized contact, I’d prefer fewer, more targeted interventions to avoid wasting advisor time and student annoyance.
S2.Q8.1: It would be good to know how the model handles students who are already receiving support services – to avoid duplication or conflicting advice.

S3.notes.Q3: Privacy is crucial, but disability *could* improve identification without being overly invasive. Still cautious about broad data collection. Unequal application would be terrible.
S3.notes.Q4: Explainability is important, especially for students already vulnerable. A little loss of accuracy is acceptable if it means understanding *why* a decision was made.
S3.notes.Q5: Fairness is paramount, even with a small reduction in overall effectiveness. Missing students from marginalized groups would worsen existing problems.
S3.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach feels less intrusive and allows for a real conversation. Frequent check-ins could be overwhelming, twice yearly seems sensible.
S3.notes.Q7: Less selective contact with just general info is okay. But personalized emails require a balance - don’t want to overload advisors or falsely alarm students.
S3.Q8.1: The survey doesn't address the potential for the model to *reinforce* existing biases in support access, only that it shouldn’t create new ones. It feels like those are two separate concerns.

S4.notes.Q3: Privacy is paramount, but disability info *could* help equalize things if it really makes a difference in fairness. Don't want to build profiles based on potentially sensitive characteristics.
S4.notes.Q4: Explainability matters a LOT, especially given my own experiences navigating support systems with ADHD. Need to understand *why* I’m getting flagged. Less accuracy is okay for more transparency.
S4.notes.Q5: Fairness is essential, even if it means reaching fewer students overall. Making sure marginalized groups aren't further disadvantaged outweighs boosting the total number helped.
S4.notes.Q6: A personalized touch is crucial – generic emails get lost. I'd be more likely to engage with a specific invite than just general info. Twice a year feels reasonable.
S4.notes.Q7: Over-contacting is annoying and can feel invasive. Prioritize quality over quantity, particularly with personalized outreach; a balance seems right when there’s a more tailored response.
S4.Q8.1: It feels important to have an 'opt out' option for students - being identified by a model could be stressful for some, even if it is meant to help.

S5.notes.Q3: I'm wary of invasive data, but some (nationality, first-gen status) might be relevant for understanding barriers to success and addressing inequalities if used carefully.
S5.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for trust, especially as an international student navigating a new system. I want to understand *why* the model flags me. Losing accuracy is acceptable if it means transparency.
S5.notes.Q5: Fairness needs to be a priority; perpetuating inequalities isn't okay. I'd rather miss some students than unfairly disadvantage already marginalized groups.
S5.notes.Q6: A personalized approach is much more welcoming and useful than a generic email. A meeting would be good, but it needs to be truly optional.
S5.notes.Q7: For a simple notification, contacting lots of students is fine. But with personalized advice, being too broad feels intrusive. A balance feels right.
S5.Q8.1: I’m concerned about how this system might interact with the cultural differences I'm experiencing as an international student. Assumptions made by the model could be based on norms different from my own.

S6.notes.Q3: Privacy is key, but some data *can* help if it genuinely improves reach to struggling students. Nationality/first-gen status are relevant due to potential integration challenges.
S6.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial for building trust, especially given my own experience restarting studies in a new country. Less accuracy isn't worth it if no one understands why.
S6.notes.Q5: Fairness is vital, and I’d rather reach fewer students *equally* than more with bias. Missing some isn't great but it's better than reinforcing existing inequalities.
S6.notes.Q6: Personalized outreach feels less intrusive and more supportive than generic emails. A meeting allows for nuanced discussion of needs.
S6.notes.Q7: With a personalized approach, it's okay to be more selective – the quality of outreach matters more than quantity. Blanket emails are less helpful.
S6.Q8.1: It feels like there isn’t enough consideration for students who’ve already dropped out once - what safeguards would prevent unnecessary contact after they’ve made that decision?

S7.notes.Q3: Privacy is important, but acknowledging disability feels less invasive if it helps ensure fairness in support. Other demographic data feels too personal for this.
S7.notes.Q4: Explainability is crucial, especially with my dyslexia. Need to understand *why* I'm flagged, not just that I am. Losing some accuracy for clarity feels right.
S7.notes.Q5: Fairness is key! It’s unacceptable if the system disadvantages already vulnerable groups, even to get a few more identifications overall. Recall feels more important than avoiding false positives.
S7.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel useless; personalization shows you're paying attention. A meeting is good, but should always be voluntary. Twice a year strikes a balance.
S7.notes.Q7: With personalized outreach, fewer contacts are okay as long as it’s targeted and helpful. Mass emails risk overwhelming students who don't need them.
S7.Q8.1: The survey doesn’t address how the model will be updated or audited for bias over time. Constant monitoring is crucial to prevent unfair outcomes.

S8.notes.Q3: I'm wary of data collection, especially anything too personal. My own dropout experience makes me sensitive to being 'tracked'. First-gen status or financial aid *might* be okay if it improves fairness, but only then.
S8.notes.Q4: Explainability is important for trust, but I'm willing to trade *some* of it for better identification, especially moving from moderate to low explainability. But no one should be flagged without any ability to understand why.
S8.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial. I don’t want the system to reinforce existing inequalities, even if it means fewer students are identified overall. Prioritising equal recall feels right.
S8.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal and ineffective, given my own experience. A personalized email *and* an invitation to a meeting seem like the most supportive options. Twice a year strikes a balance.
S8.notes.Q7: For basic info, contacting more students is okay – low risk. But with personalized support, it’s important to avoid overwhelming advisors and the students themselves.
S8.Q8.1: I worry about the potential for a self-fulfilling prophecy. If a student is flagged as ‘at risk’, will that negatively impact their confidence and performance? And how will this data be used *after* university?

S9.notes.Q3: Privacy is crucial, especially with sensitive data. Improvement needs to be substantial for me to accept wider data usage. Disability *should* be considered for fairness but requires careful handling.
S9.notes.Q4: Explainability is really important. I need to understand why the model flags me, especially with my health condition. A little less accuracy for more transparency is worth it.
S9.notes.Q5: Fairness is non-negotiable. It’s unacceptable if the model disadvantages certain groups, even to improve overall results. Prioritizing recall ensures everyone gets help.
S9.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal. Personalized outreach, maybe with an invite to chat, feels more supportive. Constant contact would be overwhelming.
S9.notes.Q7: With generic info, a wider net is ok. But for personalized advice, the risk of misidentification is higher so fewer contacts are better.
S9.Q8.1: The survey doesn’t explicitly address how data will be anonymized/protected long-term. What about data breaches and re-identification risks?
